claims.text: A GPU-accelerated, actively learned neural-network potential can reliably replace full ab initio molecular dynamics for calculating solid and liquid free energies.
The surrogate can retain vibrational, anharmonic, and electron-vibration contributions relevant to fusion thermodynamics.
Multicomponent systems near melting can exhibit complex high-temperature structural and chemical behavior in disordered or partially molten states.
The relevant free-energy landscapes of elemental, binary, and multicomponent systems include anharmonic and electron-vibration effects.
The neural-network potential should be trained on strategically sampled ab initio data selected through active learning.
On-the-fly corrections during free-energy integration can ensure accurate treatment of key entropy contributions.
The method is applicable from just below the melting temperature to approximately 1.2 times the melting temperature.
The method is applicable to elemental, binary, and high-entropy systems containing up to approximately five constituents.
The learned potential can accurately reproduce the ab initio free-energy landscape in both solid and fluid phases.
Learning interactions from a limited number of high-fidelity ab initio simulations is sufficient to achieve fidelity close to direct molecular dynamics.
Adaptive corrections during integration can substantially reduce computational cost without sacrificing phase-free-energy accuracy.
ML-computed free energies will agree with full ab initio molecular-dynamics results to within approximately 10 meV per atom.
The proposed workflow can reduce computational cost by up to roughly one order of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed workflow can overcome TOR-TILD inefficiencies in multicomponent high-entropy systems.
Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy workflows are computationally expensive, while TOR-TILD becomes slow for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
Performance outside the specified composition and temperature limits is uncertain.
Cost reduction and fidelity may depend on system complexity and training-set diversity.
The ability of on-the-fly corrections to capture strongly nonlinear anharmonic and electron-vibration interactions remains unvalidated.

contradictions.description: The prediction loosely associates the ±10 meV/atom tolerance with free energies and derived observables such as melting temperature, but an energy-per-atom tolerance is not dimensionally applicable to melting temperature, and no separate temperature-error threshold is supplied.

The hypothesis emphasizes overcoming TOR-TILD inefficiency in multicomponent systems, but the proposed decisive benchmark uses only an elemental or binary system and compares primarily against full ab initio MD, so it cannot decisively test the multicomponent or TOR-TILD performance claim.
